title: ADHD Therapy After an Evaluation: Choosing the Next Step
description: Simple next steps after an ADHD evaluation. Learn how to compare therapy options, what to ask, and how to choose a provider.
main_html:
What this guide is best for

Direct answer: Start with the evaluation's recommendations, choose one daily difficulty you want help with, and ask a therapist how their approach addresses it. Confirm who provides therapy, who handles any medication discussion, and how the people involved will coordinate before booking a course of appointments.

Best used when: You have an ADHD evaluation report and need to turn the recommendations into a practical first appointment for yourself or your child.

Quick answer

An evaluation and a therapy plan answer different questions. The report explains the findings and recommendations; a therapy conversation turns the relevant recommendations into goals, sessions and a way to review whether the support is helping. You do not have to solve every difficulty before making that first call. Bring the report and identify the situation that is causing the most trouble now.

The CDC's information on adult ADHD describes treatment as potentially including medication, therapy or other behavioral approaches, with follow-up and adjustments according to the person. A diagnosis does not automatically select one service or guarantee that the clinician who evaluated you also provides ongoing treatment.

Read the recommendations with the evaluator

Sort the recommendations by next contact

Before shopping for another assessment, ask for the feedback appointment or clarification of the report you already have. Mark recommendations that you understand, those you want explained, and those that need someone else to act. Separate a suggestion about therapy from a suggestion about school, work or a prescriber. They may involve different contacts and different paperwork.

Write down what prompted the evaluation in the first place. For an adult, that might be unfinished work, recurring missed appointments or conflict around household tasks. For a child, it might be a repeated difficulty with routines or schoolwork. Ask the evaluator which findings relate to that specific problem and which recommendations should be discussed first. If a recommendation is outside the report's scope, ask who can answer it.

Arrange a secure report handover

Ask whether the therapist needs the complete report or a summary, how to share it securely, and whether you need to sign a release. Keep your own copy of the report and the feedback notes. Do not assume a referral transfers records automatically or that an appointment system has connected the two offices.

Match the service to the age and the goal

Check what the service actually includes

Ask the provider to describe the approach they would discuss for this age group and situation, what happens in a session, and what practice outside sessions involves. “We treat ADHD” is a starting point for questions, not an explanation of the service. You should be able to describe the proposed work in ordinary words after the call.

Ask about age-specific experience

For children, the CDC's behavior therapy guidance describes the role of parent training and support with behavior. Ask who attends, whether caregivers are taught strategies to use between visits, and how the therapist coordinates with the school when appropriate. Ask how the plan will account for the child's age rather than assuming an adult service can simply be made shorter.

For an adult seeking help with planning, ask what the therapist would do with a real example: a task that does not get started, a calendar that is not checked, or a routine that breaks down when work changes. Ask how the approach handles setbacks. If the proposed service is coaching rather than therapy, ask about the practitioner's credentials, scope and referral process; do not assume the labels mean the same thing.

A medication consultation is a separate question for a qualified prescriber. Ask who would provide it and how the therapist communicates relevant information with your permission. This guide does not decide whether medication or a particular therapy fits your circumstances.

Questions to ask on the first call

  • Do you work with people of this age who have ADHD, and what does your usual first appointment involve?
  • Will you read the evaluation before we meet? If not, how will you use its recommendations?
  • What goals would we agree on, and how would we review progress?
  • Who attends sessions, and how is time divided between the child, caregiver or other people involved?
  • Is there work between appointments, and what happens when the person cannot complete it?
  • How are questions handled between visits, and what is outside that contact arrangement?
  • Can you coordinate with the evaluator, a prescriber or the school, and what consent do you need?

Record the answers rather than trying to remember several introductory calls. Include the name of the clinician who would actually see you, the first available appointment, the location or telehealth arrangement, and the next step. A conversation with a scheduling team may still leave clinical questions unanswered; ask when and with whom those questions can be discussed.

Separate the evaluation bill from ongoing treatment

Get the ongoing appointment terms

A completed assessment does not tell you the cost of continuing visits. Ask for the intake charge, the session length and charge, the expected appointment frequency to discuss, and any separate charge for letters or coordination. Ask what happens if you need to cancel or if the clinician is unavailable. Keep a written account of what the office says is included.

Verify your own coverage questions

If you plan to use insurance, confirm the individual clinician's participation and the service with both the office and the plan. Ask about referral requirements, any authorization step, and how you can check your own responsibility before appointments begin. A provider saying they can give you a receipt does not establish what your plan will reimburse.

For out-of-network care, ask what paperwork the office supplies and who submits it. Put unanswered coverage questions on the call list before agreeing to repeated appointments. Compare the same service and session length across offices rather than comparing an evaluation package with a therapy session.

Choose an observable goal for the first review

Instead of “be more organized,” bring an example such as “start the homework routine with fewer repeated prompts” or “use one agreed place to check tomorrow's appointments.” These are examples to discuss with the therapist, not a prescribed treatment exercise. Ask what would be a reasonable first goal, what you will observe, and when you will revisit it together.

Keep brief notes on what happened, what support was available and what got in the way. Include occasions when a strategy helped as well as when it did not. The review can then focus on whether the plan fits the real environment, whether instructions are clear and whether another problem needs attention. A difficult week is information for that conversation, not a reason to hide the notes.

Agree on what to do if sessions feel confusing or the practical arrangements stop working. Ask who to contact about a concern, whether the plan can be reviewed, and how a handover would work if a different service becomes appropriate. Knowing that route before a difficulty arises makes follow-up easier.

What to do next

Put the report, your feedback questions, one daily-life example and the scheduling or coverage answers in one place. Choose a first appointment based on the service and follow-up you understand. For local options, use the city directory alongside the provider questions above; a listing alone cannot establish fit.

Bring remaining questions back to the evaluator or prospective treating clinician. Educational only. Not medical advice. No endorsements or rankings, and no promise of a particular treatment outcome.
meta_title: ADHD Therapy After an Evaluation: Choosing the Next Step

search_strengthening.definition: ADHD therapy after an evaluation is the treatment step that follows a diagnosis: behavioural therapy or parent training for children, cognitive behavioural therapy and skills coaching for adults, often alongside a medication discussion with a prescriber. The evaluation report is the starting point, because its recommendations say which kind of therapy fits.

faq.q: What happens after an ADHD evaluation?
faq.a: You receive a report and a feedback session that explain the findings and recommend next steps. Those recommendations usually point to therapy, school or workplace accommodations, a medication consultation, or a combination.

faq.q: What kind of therapy helps ADHD?
faq.a: For children, parent training and behavioural therapy are the usual first step. For teens and adults, cognitive behavioural therapy and organisational skills coaching are common. The evaluation report should say which fits.

faq.q: What should I ask a therapist after an ADHD diagnosis?
faq.a: Ask whether they treat ADHD specifically, which approach they use, how they will measure progress, how they coordinate with a prescriber or school, and what sessions cost with your insurance.
